job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In the bustling city of Vidyut Nagar, local electrician Mr. Sharma was inspecting a household circuit after a minor power surge. He explained to his young apprentice that a battery is actually a combination of two or more cells connected together, rather than just a single cell. He pointed to the circuit diagram, noting that the long, thin line in the cell symbol represents the positive terminal. While inspecting the wiring, he highlighted the importance of the electric fuse. He clarified that a fuse is a safety device designed to melt and break the circuit when current exceeds a safe limit, rather than slowing down the flow of electricity. He also demonstrated how an electromagnet works by wrapping a wire around an iron nail. He explained that an electromagnet is a temporary magnet that only functions when electricity flows through the coil. To increase the magnetic strength, he added more turns of wire to the coil, explaining that more turns create a stronger magnetic field. Finally, he reminded his apprentice that current is not consumed by the bulb; instead, the same amount of current that enters the bulb leaves it, having simply converted electrical energy into light and heat.

items.evidence: He clarified that a fuse is a safety device designed to melt and break the circuit when current exceeds a safe limit, rather than slowing down the flow of electricity.
items.q: Too much current suddenly flows in a house circuit. What does the fuse do?
options: Its wire melts and cuts off the current
It slows the current down to a safe level
It sends the extra current back to the cell
Its wire gets thicker to carry more current
items.explain: A fuse melts and breaks the circuit when current is too high; it does not slow current.

wrong.why: thinks a fuse slows down the current
imagines extra current is stored or returned
thinks a thicker fuse wire is safer

items.evidence: He explained that an electromagnet is a temporary magnet that only functions when electricity flows through the coil.
items.q: Mr. Sharma switches off the current to his coiled iron nail. What happens to the nail?
options: It stops behaving like a magnet
It stays a magnet, since it was started
It gets stronger as the wire cools down
It attracts only things touching the wire
items.explain: An electromagnet is temporary; it works only while electricity flows through the coil.

wrong.why: thinks electricity only starts a permanent magnet
thinks magnetic effect needs touching the wire

items.evidence: To increase the magnetic strength, he added more turns of wire to the coil, explaining that more turns create a stronger magnetic field.
items.q: Coil A has 20 turns and coil B has 50 turns on the same nail. Which is stronger?
options: Coil B, as extra turns add strength
Coil A, as electricity travels a shorter path
Coil A, as fewer turns use less current
Coil B, but only after the current stops
items.explain: More turns of wire make a stronger magnetic field, so the 50-turn coil is stronger.

wrong.why: thinks a longer path makes the magnet weaker
thinks the coil uses up current
thinks an electromagnet works without current

items.evidence: Finally, he reminded his apprentice that current is not consumed by the bulb; instead, the same amount of current that enters the bulb leaves it, having simply converted electrical energy into light and heat.
items.q: Some current flows into a glowing bulb. How much current comes out of the other side?
options: The same amount that went in
Less, as the bulb uses some up
More, as light and heat are added
None, as it all turns into light
items.explain: The bulb does not use up current; the same current leaves it, only energy changes form.

wrong.why: thinks the bulb consumes some current
reverses the idea, thinks light adds current
confuses current with energy turned into light
